speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: REQUEST FROM BRITISH MINISTRY FOR INCREASED SHIPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before motions are called I should like to make a statement to the house with regard to a development in connection with food requirements which I think should be made known not only to the house but to the country.
Yesterday, October 3, about noon, I had a phone call from Sir Ben Smith, British Minister. of Food. The telephone call was to acquaint me with the fact that the food position in Great Britain at the present time is more difficult than at any time since the beginning of the war, and making an appeal to us to help in any way that we possibly can in connection with supplying one particular kind of food, namely bacon.
He stated in that telephone conversation that unless something could be done during the next two months it would be necessary in Great Britain to reduce the ration from three ounces to two ounces per week. It will be recalled by hon. members that the ration throughout the greater part of the war stood at four ounces, and during a considerable part of it the amount was higher than that. But toward the end of the war it became necessary to reduce the ration to three ounces. It is now

Bacon-Increased Shipments ______
suggested that unless within the next two months we can do something to assist, it will be necessary to reduce that ration to two ounces. The cause of this, of course, lies in the fact that Great Britain has been doing everything possible to assist in building up the supplies of food on the continent which are necessary to maintain conditions there.
When that appeal was made I directed the meat board to make a study of our position in Canada, and to communicate further with them in connection with the matter. Through the further communications we have thought it wise to suggest to the British government that an attempt will be made in Canada to increase our shipments of bacon to Great Britain over the next two months.
Our present dommitments or allocations require 11,000 tons in October and 11,000 in November. The suggestion is that if we could increase that amount by 3,000 tons in October and 3,000 in November they could continue their three-ounce ration during those two months, and that probably after that they would be able to take care of the situation. We had suggested to them that we would probably find no difficulty in continuing the
11.000	tons for October, and in increasing to
18.000	tons for November. They came back, however, with the suggestion that it would be most difficult for them to carry on throughout November unless we could increase our shipments in October.
So, Mr. Speaker, what I wish to say to the house, and to the people of Canada generally, is that we believe that if we all cooperate we can make these shipments possible. We anticipate no difficulty from the producers, because we are just now entering upon the period of greatest shipments or greatest marketings of farm products, particularly hogs. We believe that while the hog deliveries will be slightly lower than they were a year ago, sufficient hogs will be coming into the market to make these shipments possible. In the next place it will be necessary for us to operate our packing plants to capacity during that period of time; and in the third place it will be necessary to have available the shipping facilities which will take to the point where it is required the fullest amount we can possibly supply to the market. We do not anticipate any difficulty in connection with shipping facilities or with refrigeration. There can be very little difficulty in the matter of getting the facilities necessary in that direction. So we have undertaken to do everything possible to see to it that this bacon is advanced to the British

within the next two months in an increased amount of 6,000 tons over and above what we had previously been expecting to ship.
I am sure that in making this known to the house and to the country I do not need to make any further appeal than the appeal that has been made by the Minister of Food in Great Britain. I believe it is not only in the interests of humanity that we should send forward the product, but it is in our own interests as a country which is going to have products to sell that we should be able to meet this, which may be the last, appeal made to us to do something a little in advance of what we thought we would be able to do in order to bring to a most successful conclusion our activities in connection with the supplying of food to the European continent during and after war. I believe that every effort will be made to see to it that this product is sent forward.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF THANKS ON BEHALF OF GOVERNMENT OF UNITED KINGDOM

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker, I think the house will be interested in hearing the contents of a very gracious telegram which was received on September 30 from the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs. It is as follows:
From the Secretary of.. State for Dominion Affairs
To the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Canada
London, September 29, 1945.
No. 204. Now that almost all the children evacuated to Canada under the children's overseas reception board scheme have reurned to the United Kingdom, I wish, on behalf of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, to express our grateful thanks to His Majesty's government in Canada and to all those foster parents, officials, school teachers and private citizens throughout Canada who have cared for these children so generously and sympathetically during the past five years.
It will never be forgotten that in the time of our great need you welcomed our children into your homes, and not only fed and clothed and educated them, but gave them that patient care and thoughtful guidance which only parents or the best of friends can give.
We realize that the responsibility for these guests from overseas must have pressed heavily on the foster parents at times, especially as the strain of war increased and they had to contend with their own anxieties and problems. Their patience, and that of the officials and social agencies, has never failed, and to that has been added kindness and generosity of countless Canadians who have given freely of their skill, their time and their money to make the Children's stay both memorable and happy.
For all this inestimable kindness and generosity, I thank you all most sincerely on behalf of the United Kingdom government and of the parents. Some of our boys and girls have elected to make their homes with you. and we are proud to think that a number have served in the Canadian forces. All are bringing back happy memories of their five years in Canada, and links which have been forged as a result of your hospitality between so many homes in our two countries are based upon real affection as well as of gratitude.
Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs.
To that gracious telegram the following reply was sent:
From the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, Ottawa
To the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, London
No. 227	Ottawa, October: 2, 1945.
Your telegram No. 204 of September 29. On behalf of the government of Canada I express to you our cordial appreciation of your message of thanks for the reception accorded in Canada to the children evacuated from the United Kingdom under the children's overseas reception

board scheme. Your message is being made public here and I am sure that it will be much appreciated by all those in this country who were associated with the care of the Children during the last five years. The imminent dangers which led to the evacuation have passed into memory, we hope never to return. The successful execution of the scheme leaves behind it new and close ties between many families in our two countries and warm friendships which will endure. We are glad that some of those who came to Canada under the scheme will remain with us.
Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON MARKETING-REMOVAL OF 14-BUSHEL LIMITATION FOR PRESENT CROP YEAR,

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON MARKETING-REMOVAL OF 14-BUSHEL LIMITATION FOR PRESENT CROP YEAR,
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about two weeks ago I made a statement to the house on wheat prices. At that time I should have liked to be able to deal further with the marketing of wheat, but finality had not been reached at that time. To-day I should like to give the house a statement on the very important matter of wheat marketing. It is a little longer than I should have liked it to be, but I ivant to get the facts in connection with this matter on the record.
Since the crop year 1941-42, the government's wheat programme has included a restriction on the total quantity of wheat to be marketed within any one crop year. In view of the present wheat position, the origin and purpose of the restriction on wheat marketings might be carefully explained.
The following circumstances led to the adoption of a policy of restricting the volume of wheat to be marketed within any one crop year and the volume of wheat to be marketed by any single producer during the same period:
1.	In the early years of the war, overseas markets for Canadian wheat were limited and consisted mainly of the requirements for the United Kingdom. Even shipments of wheat to t-he United Kingdom remained at a fairly low level owing to the submarine menace and the shortage of shipping in those days. There was, therefore, no opportunity to market all the surplus wheat which resulted from the large crops harvested in 1939 and 1940.
2.	On July 31, 1940, the carry-over of Canadian wheat was 300 million bushels, and the 1940 wheat crop was estimated at 514 million bushels for the prairie provinces, making total supplies of over 800 million .bi/ihels for the crop year 1940-41, with a prospective export market of about 230 million bushels. The

Wheat Marketing Statement
1940-41 programme provided for seasonal delivery quotas but no over-all restriction on the marketing of wheat. Consequently, the government took the necessary steps to see that producers had an opportunity of marketing all of the wheat which they desired to market in the crop year 1940-41. During the crop year, producers delivered 456 million bushels of wheat and at the end of the crop year; very little remained) on farms. Marketing of the entire 1940 wheat crop was only possible because arrangements were made to provide temporary storage facilities both at the lakehead and at country elevator points.
When the grain policy for the succeeding crop year, 1941-42, was under discussion, it appeared that the carry-over of wheat at July 31, 1941 would be in the neighbourhood of 500 million bushels, practically all in the licensed storage facilities of this country which in pre-war days had a capacity of some 450 million bushels. This meant that country elevators would be congested at the start of the new crop year and the physical ability to take delivery of wheat was severely restricted.
3.	Under these circumstances the suggestion was advanced in western Canada from responsible quarters that the government should permit the marketing of that amount of wheat which could be sold at home or abroad during the crop year 1941, and the stockpile as at July 31, 1941, should be carried as a war-time reserve. This suggestion was accepted by the government, and the 1941-42 grain programme included a restriction of marketings to 230 million bushels-an estimate of the volume of wheat which could be disposed of in domestic and export markets during the crop year 1941-42.
4.	Having arrived at an absolutely safe position in respect to quantities of wheat required in the prosecution of the war, it was becoming increasingly evident that war-time demand was gravitating to live stock and live stock products. This demand came not only from the United Kingdom and from our growing armed forces, but from the domestic market which had been expanding steadily. The government, therefore, decided that positive steps should be taken to increase the production of live stock and live stock products, necessitating an increase in feed grain production. To that end the Wheat Acreage Reduction Act of 1941 provided financial benefits for the diversion of wheat acreage to other grains and summer-fallow, which proved to be effective.
The same basic wheat situation and livestock situation continued in Canada in the succeeding years, and the limitation on wheat
marketings has remained an important feature of the dominion government's wheat policy in each crop year since 1941-42.
The necessity of this provision is indicated by the following table, which shows the carryover of Canadian wheat, annual production in the prairie provinces, and total available supplies for the four crop	years from	1941-42 to1944-45:	July 31,	TotalStocks	New crop	supplies(Million bushels)	1941-42	... 480	296	7761942-43....	. . . 424	528	9521943-44	... 595	268	8631944-45. ...	... 356	411	767
During this period, carryover figures ranged from 355 million bushels in 1944-45 to 595 million bushels on July 31, 1943. Total supplies of wheat in Canada ranged from 952 million bushels in 1942-43 to 776 million bushels in 1941-42. These figures indicate the extent to which war-time reserves of wheat were continuously carried in Canada and the enormous quantities available in relation to immediate needs. It is obvious that without over-all restriction of marketings a situation might have arisen, and in fact did arise in 1942-43, where it was impossible to take delivery of all wheat offered by producers. The limitation on marketings provided the basis upon which all producers would share alike in any quantity of wheat which could be marketed within any one crop year. Otherwise, marketing opportunity would have been available in the first instance to producers at delivery points where grain storage happened to be more adequate.
Throughout the years under review, and even down to the present crop year, the government has never advocated expansion in wheat acreage, but on the contrary has advocated the maintenance and expansion where possible of the production of live stock and live stock products. This does not mean that the government did not recognize the necessity of maintaining a large volume of wheat for importing countries when the war in Europe ended. The figures which I have quoted indicate the extent to which this objective was kept in mind throughout the years. On D-day about 300 million bushels of wheat were available in Canada with the 1944 harvest sixty days away. On V-E day about 320 million bushels of wheat were on hand, with substantial quantities still to be delivered by producers prior to July 31, 1945, and the 1945 crop not far away. We had these supplies after providing the United States with over 160 million bushels of wheat in 1943-44 to supplement their feed grain supplies.
Wheat Marketing Statement

Early in 1943 the market situation improved largely because of the large imports required by the United States. But at this point a new factor entered the grain picture. This was the difficulty of securing sufficient transportation to move the quantities of wheat and feed grains required in the domestic market and in the export market. Since that time, transportation has been the controlling factor in the volume of wheat and other grains which could be made available for export. In 194344, in the fifth year of the war, the railways were called upon practically to double the volume of transportation available for the movement of grain, and even with these increased transportation facilities it was very difficult to keep up with available demand at all times. Since the crop year 1943-44 we have always had to bear in mind that the transportation factor had to be considered as well as the current and prospective demand. Not only were there large quantities of wheat to move, but by this time we were producing large surpluses of feed grains which had to be distributed in deficit areas in Canada and in the United States, and transportation became a vital consideration in the government's grain policy.
When policy was under discussion for the crop year 1945-46 we felt that the transportation situation was such that we would have a carryover of wheat on July 31, 1945, of about 325 million bushels, the equivalent of about a full year's export under the then existing conditions. We thought that a small crop of, say, 300 million bushels would give us total wheat supplies of over 600 million bushels in addition to 150 to 200 million bushels of marketed feed grains, or total supplies which would press upon the capacity of our railroads and port facilities having regard to other forms of war-time traffic which they were carrying. We also realized that if the 1945 crop were a large crop we would have to face extremely difficult conditions in respect to the movement of marketed grain. This fact, accompanied by the intensification of the demand for feed grains and live stock and live stock products, provided ample grounds for retaining the over-all marketing restriction in 1945-46. We also had another important consideration in mind. We knew we had on hand a very large volume of wheat which could be used to meet overseas requirements in case the war ended; all the wheat which Canada, as one of the wheat exporting countries of the world, could be excepted to carry to meet early post-war requirements.
In one respect our calculation of our wheat position early in 1945 was not borne out by subsequent events. V-E day resulted in the

raising of exports in the crop year 1944-45 by about 65 million bushels, and the reduction in our July 31 stocks from an anticipated 325 million to 258 million bushels, with, of course, some of the post-war European demand already met. The 1945 prairie wheat crop has turned out to be a crop of moderate size-some 300 million bushels. Whereas we expected wheat supplies of perhaps 650 million bushels for the crop year 1945-46, our total supplies will aggregate about 550 million bushels, with an additional 170 million bushels of feed grains to be marketed and transported during the present crop year. The supply of some 150 million bushels less wheat than we expected early in 1945 will, none tne less, tax the capacity of our railroads during the first half of the present crop year, and particularly our ability to move grain through available Canadian and United States ports.
During the present crop year we expect to export about 325 million bushels of wheat, leaving between 75 to 100 million bushels of wheat on hand July 31, 1946. Since V-E day over one-half of the wheat going into Europe has been Canadian wheat, and that percentage will be fully maintained during the present crop year.
The average yield per acre in western Canada this year is not large. Most of the surplus from the 1945 crop will be marketed within the 14-bushel limitation. There are some areas, however, and many producers who will have wheat in excess of the 14-bushel delivery limitation. If the restriction on the limitation on marketings is lifted for the balance of the present crop year, it will probably mean an additional 15 million bushels of wheat available for importing countries during the present crop year. In view of the efforts which this country is making to provide food for Europe, the government feels that if a little more wheat can be provided by lifting marketing restrictions for the present crop year, this action should be taken. It has therefore been decided to remove the 14-bushel limitation for the present crop year.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO CONTINUANCE OP REDUCED PARE RESTRICTIONS
STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO CONTINUANCE OP REDUCED PARE RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
I have received representations
from various groups, associations and individuals in connection with the cancellation of reduced rates on railways over the week-end for dominion and provincial holidays, and also for parties of ten or more. I have considered these representations and I should like to make a statement to the house.
For some years it has been found necessary in order to assure the maximum use of railway facilities for the prosecution of the war to suspend or cancel certain reduced fares for holiday and excursion travel which in normal times have been afforded by the Canadian railways to the travelling public.
There are now in force the following orders:
Order in council P.C. 2557 of March 30, 1943, extended to November 15, 1945, which prohibits the sale of reduced fares for dominion or provincial holidays, weekends and parties of ten or more;
Orders of the Transport Controller:
T.C. 01P of June 24, 1942, cancelling special tariffs of reduced rates or fares covering agricultural exhibitions, celebrations, coach excursions, horse races, organized excursion parties and other special fares;
T.C. 02P of July 30, 1942, cancelling bargain fares, eastern to western Canada, prairies to pacific coast, and certain conventions;
T.C. 07P of June 25, 1943, suspending home visitors' fares and summer tourist fares.
The Canadian railways report that the movement of the armed forces is now taxing their facilities to capacity, and that in September the capacity of their equipment was exceeded. I expect that the return of service personnel from Europe to Canada will continue over the next few months in sufficient numbers to require the maximum use of all available railway trains, accommodation and operating crews. The repatriation and demobilization of the armed services place a great strain on the operation of the Canadian railways which during the war years have shouldered the increased burden of transportation demands
with vigor and efficiency. Great credit is due the railways for their important contribution to the war effort and final victory.
In addition to this expected movement, a large number of British prisoners of war and internees from the Pacific will travel across Canada, and this will take a lot of railway equipment, but it can be done advantageously by the use of sleeping car equipment returning from the Pacific coast.
During the period of demobilization it behooves the travelling public to refrain as much as possible from unnecessary railway travel on pleasure or for visits to their rela-ties until after the service movement is finished which will be about the end of next April. During the month of December, I expect that the railways will again be called upon to handle inbound troop movements through the port of Halifax, necessitating longer hauls for equipment. December is ordinarily an unusually heavy month for the railways on account of Christmas holiday travel, and the additional movement of service personnel may tax the railways beyond the capacity of their equipment.
It is with regret that I have to announce that there will be no removal of the restrictions now in effect on reduced fares for railway travel until after January 1, 1946, when the whole question will again be reviewed. I hope to be able to announce the lifting of the restrictions on reduced fares by the middle of January, but of course this will depend upon the traffic conditions prevailing at that time.

subtopic: REVERSION ON NOVEMBER 1 TO PRE-WAR HOURS OF WORK
REVERSION ON NOVEMBER 1 TO PRE-WAR HOURS OF WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the second of July last one-half of the extra hour which the members of the civil service had been working during the war was restored to them. It has now been decided that, effective on November 1, the civil service will return to its pre-war hours of work.
The net result of the change will be that the extra hour which the civil service worked during the war will now be returned to them.
In view of transportation difficulties it will be necessary to retain staggered hours of arrival and departure where these are at present in effect, for the time being at any rate.
The government, and I am sure the house generally, wishes to express its wholehearted appreciation to the members of the public service for their work during the war. Many have come to Ottawa from all parts of Canada

for several years of strenuous service in the war effort. Many have been loaned by industry; many have left their household duties, or their well-earned leisure hours of retirement, to take their place in civil service ranks.
The permanent civil service has accomplished a splendid piece of work during the war. To all these the government and the house expresses its sincere appreciation and gratitude.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time for the purpose of asking leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the adjournment of the house, under standing order 31, for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the strike at the Ford plant at Windsor, Ontario, affecting some ten thousand employees, and the danger of this strike, if not settled immediately, spreading to other automobile plants and affecting a total of some thirty thousand employees and ultimately involving workers in other industrial plants throughout the

country. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that if you doubt the urgency of the matter you will use your discretionary power to allow the house to decide.

Mr. Speaker, on the matter
of urgency, this industrial dispute in Windsor is the first of our post-war difficulties in the field of labour relations. The attitude of the government in this regard may determine future labour relations in the very difficult period in the transition from war to peace. The urgency, sir, is on the following grounds. First, the strike has the city of Windsor tied up with ten thousand employees of the Ford Motor company involved. There are some thirty thousand workers in similar plants, under the same union, who have taken a strike vote and are standing by. They decided by a ninety per cent vote at least that if and when it was demonstrated to them that action on their part was necessary they would join the Ford strike, with immediate strike action. I am afraid that if some action is not taken by the government immediately we may find ourselves, perhaps this time next week, with all the automotive industry tied up, and, in addition to that, other plants across this country which are unionized, perhaps utilizing their affiliation, through the congress of labour and other bodies, to take similar action in support of the Ford workers. The hon. member for Temiscouata called attention to the words in standing order 12 which state that Mr. Speaker shall decide questions of order, subject to an appeal to the house without debate. The Minister of Mines and Resources asserts that that does not apply to standing order 31, because in his opinion the decision Your Honour made on the hon. member's request was not on a point of order. But he himself-the minister -quoted paragraph 3 of standing order 31 a number of times, which has in it these words: "who"-referring to Mr. Speaker- "if he thinks it in order"-and so on. I submit that it was your opinion that the request of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), seconded by myself, was not in order. That is the crux of the matter now under discussion, namely that the request was out of order.
I know that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), who is leading the house, has already quoted decisions made by Speakers in previous parliaments, and has pointed out the fact that those decisions were upheld by votes of the house. But I find nowhere in the book of rules any order to the effect that Speakers' decisions, even if upheld by votes of the house, become rules of the house. It seems to me that the only thing that is binding, or that carries from one parliament to another, is the set of standing orders themselves.
On many occasions I have endeavoured to quote citations contained in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, and have been told that those really do not hold. It has been pointed out to me that only the precise standing orders count. If the citations contained in this book do not count, or do not hold, then surely the decisions of previous parliaments are not binding upon this parliament. I submit it is our right to decide that standing order 12, which gives the house the right, of appeal from a Speaker's ruling on a point of order, definitely includes standing order 31, because it says:
. . . Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:

He said; His Honour the Deputy of the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.
I would like to place myself in the hands of the house with regard to this resolution. In order to explain why, may I say that at the meeting held at Hot Springs, I think in 1943, a decision was made to set up a conference on food and matters pertaining to food. The first meeting of that conference is to be held in Quebec beginning on October 16. It is urgent that between now and October 16 we should become parties to that arrangement by the passing of a measure based on this resolution.
This legislation is made necessary as a result of the fact that more than twenty nations have agreed to become part of that conference-twenty was the figure set at Hot Springs. Twenty-eight countries have asked for the privilege of operating under this arrangement. We hope to bring down the legislation next week. The only reason it was not brought down earlier is that we have been dealing with other matters that had been arranged for at the beginning of the session. I would like to ask the permission of the house to allow this resolution to go into committee and to pass its second reading to that stage to-day, and then whatever discussion we wish to have on the matter could take place on the second reading of the bill, which I would hope to have brought down next Tuesday. This committee should be informed as to just what is being done in connection with this agreement for a food and agriculture organization. Who is to be in charge of it? What do each of the twenty nations contribute, and how is it administered as to China? What food is to be given? A report has been made by the American Red Cross bearing on this matter. I called the attention of the Prime Minister to it in the debate on external affairs in August of 1944, and he said that he would look into it.
My next point is that parliament should be informed of what Canada and the other countries are going to do under this agreement. We shall have to vote the money. Where are the supplies going? From what I have heard, some supplies destined to China did not reach China at all. What about transportation from North America across the seas? Who is in charge of that? School teachers are all right teaching school and in many other ways; in fact, some of our best leaders have been drawn from that class. But we should have in charge of this business someone who has a practical knowledge of food products, live stock, transportation, expert administration, and so forth. I ask the minister who is in charge, because the Prime Minister is not here. I want to see the resolution go through, but I ask that a proper survey be made along the lines I have indicated and that the public be informed, because the public will have to pay. I am in favour of this step to send food and supplies to suffering peoples, but in this matter we should act as business men. We are voting hundreds of millions of dollars; where is the money coming from? It is coming out of current revenue. Parliament should be informed of just what is to be done. That a select committee be appointed, 1. 2. To prepare and bring in one or more bills to clarify, amend or supplement the above legislation;
With power to send for persons, papers, and records; to print its proceedings, and to report from time to time to the house;

Adamson, Ashby, Baker, Belzile, Benidickson, Bentley, Blair, Blanchette, Bridges, Brooks, Bruce, Claxton, Cleaver, Cockeram, Croll, Cruiefcshank, Dion (Lake St. John-Roberval), Dorion, Drope, Emmerson. He said: When I gave notice last evening of this resolution I informed the house that it was not my intention to debate it at this stage. As hon. gentlemen will observe from the order paper, a committee is suggested for

the approval of the house of sixty members, ex-service men of both wars, I think a very able committee, who have a tremendous task of work ahead of them on behalf of this parliament. Hon. members who were here in the last parliament will recall how sincerely and strenuously former committees of this house laboured in our committee rooms, without any trace or tinge of partisanship, and how they in the finest spirit of cooperation produced during the last five and a half years what I consider to be one of the best structures of legislation of its kind in any country of the world.
It has been a tradition of this parliament for the last twenty-five years that committees dealing with veterans' affairs be non-political and non-partisan, and those who were here before remember the work of the various committees-the pensions committee of 1941, the committee on the Veterans Land Act, the committees dealing with canteen funds, returned soldiers' insurance and various other phases of the legislation which is now before us.
Every opportunity will be presented for complete debate when the various reports reach this house and the government introduces its measures for first, second and third reading.
If hon. members will look at standing order 69 they will note that it is quite proper to have amending legislation considered by a committee of this house who will report back to the house, and for the government then to introduce its legislation.
The work of the committee will be, in the first place, to consider all the legislation since 1939, all the orders in council passed since 1939, all regulations which have been passed under statutes other than the War Measures Act, as well as under the War Measures Act since 1939-I think some of them were referred to the other day by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker)-and also to consider the administration of the legislation which we now have partly on the statute books and which we intend, after this committee's work is concluded, to have entirely on the statute books of Canada as a permanent guarantee of security for those who have been overseas, who have fought in the old war and in this one.

There is one matter that I should like to say a few words about, and that is the question of hospitalization. There are thousands of wounded men coming back at the present time. I had the honour, the opportunity and the pleasure a year ago of visiting many of our Canadian hospitals overseas, and I wish to take this occasion to pay tribute to the 
army medical corps for the splendid work it did in connection with those hospitals. I do not think there could have been anything finer. But the point I wish to make is this. As these men come back from these splendid military hospitals, let us see that the hospitals in Canada during the coming years are just as efficient and just as good.
Not long ago I read a criticism by an American colonel of the veterans hospitals in the United States after the last war. He stated, as I have stated now, that the military hospitals were the very finest, but he criticized the veterans hospitals, stating that they were in no way up to the standard that had been maintained by the military institutions. That condition may not have prevailed in this country, although on many occasions I have heard severe criticism of our veterans hospitals. But I will say again that we must give to those wounded men coming back the very finest hospitals the country can provide. We must see that they have the most competent doctors it is possible for us to place in those hospitals, and the best nurses; and other attendants must be efficient. These hospitals will be not only hospitals to these men, but, for many years to come, homes as well, and we must make them not only hospitals but homes.
The minister says the committee will be sitting for some time. I have no doubt it will be sitting for the rest of this session; I doubt if it will be able to complete its work in that time. Many things will happen before the committee makes its report, and there are thousands of young men coming back who will be looking for jobs which must be provided for them. That is something which this committee cannot look after. These young men who are going to college will benefit little, and it will do the country little good, if after three or four years in college they find that there are no suitable jobs or suitable work for them when they graduate. I would ask the minister nowT: Does he anticipate that amendments will be made to the Civil Service Act? Will that come within the terms of reference of this committee?

speechtext:
I ask this question because I think that while under the civil service commission the returned men of the last war

Pensions and Reestablishment
obtained fair treatment, there were a good many abuses. I notice, and I think it is general knowledge, that a good many of the men who took the civil service jobs took them in the low brackets, and in many cases it was not possible for them to get up to the higher brackets. I believe the Canadian legion has recommended that some system be evolved whereby these men can receive special training and help in order to fit them to advance in the civil service. That is a very good suggestion, and one which possibly might be attended to now before this committee sits, because with all the thousands of men coming back and with the reorganization and reconstruction of the civil service it may be necessary to place many of our returned men at once.
I now come to the matter of appointments which do not come under the civil service. There are many thousands of them in the gift of the dominion, provincial and municipal governments. It has been the practice too often in the past for political expediency and patronage to enter into these appointments from the very highest to the very lowest. Now that the war is over and these gallant young men are coming back, I hope that no questions of politics or patronage will enter into the appointments affecting them. That principle should start from the very highest and apply to all, down to the very lowest government appointments. May I give an example of what I have in mind? Just before the last election there was in the gift of the government the appointment of four senators and one judge from New Brunswick. To those five vacancies not one returned man was appointed. I repeat, returned men should have received consideration. I have no personal objection to the men who were appointed, except from the returned soldier's point of view. They were excellent men, and they may have had some good reason-I am sure some of them had-for not having been soldiers in the last war. However, the point is that there were returned men who were just as well qualified. If I cared to I could mention an hon. member from New Brunswick who sits in this house to-day, who served with distinction in the last war and who had three sons in the war just concluded. This man lost a son and had another one wounded. It was the expectation of the people of New Brunswick, irrespective of politics, that consideration would be given to this returned man when appointments to the senate were made. There is a great principle involved there, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that the government will take these matters into consideration.
I should now like to say a word on the question of housing. I ask the minister whether housing will come within the terms of reference of this committee?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENT OR SUPPLEMENTING OF EXISTING LEGISLATION

That also is a matter which can hardly wait for two or three months. I do not wish to labour the point this afternoon; it has been discussed many times. But we all know that veterans' housing is in a chaotic condition in Canada. There are thousands of young men coming back who are not able to buy houses for themselves and their wives. Many of these young men married overseas, and some of them have married since they returned. This matter must receive the immediate attention of the government, and not wait for reference and regulations so far as the committee is concerned.
A few weeks ago I took occasion, with some other hon. members, to visit some of those so-called veterans' houses near the city of Ottawa. I think they are totally inadequate for the purpose for which they are being built. They are too small, and too expensive, as my deskmate the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) says. I was told that they would cost between five and six thousand dollars. They are little one-storey houses containing two bedrooms. This government passed the Family Allowances Act, for what purpose? As I understood it, it was to encourage the increase of the population of Canada. Are we going to ask our soldiers who come back to this country to live in a house where there are only two bedrooms? One must be taken by the man and his wife. How many children can you put in one bedroom and expect them to be raised in the manner in which children should be brought up?
I must not take up any more of the time of the house this afternoon, but I congratulate the minister on having secured the services of General Burns as head of his rehabilitation branch. I think that is correct?

I am concerned about
that because in my capacity as a member, like all hon. members of the house, I have had many sad cases of old soldiers of the last war brought to my attention, I know that our thoughts at the moment are more particularly with the younger men who are coming home from the war just concluded; but on all sides of the house there is a keen desire that we do not forget the old soldiers of a quarter of a century ago. under that act. Many of these cases have been brought to the attention of the minister and his department over and over again. I know the members of the committee, if it is set up as the motion now stipulates, will do their work on a non-partisan basis. They will do it as veterans, out of concern for their comrades of the two wars. There is no doubt in my mind as to that. But I submit that

Pensions and Reestablishment
they start out with a handicap because of the committee's being set up in the manner the minister has proposed.
The figures have already been given-I do not know whether they have reached Hansard -as to the number of veterans in the various groups in the house. I understand there are thirty-seven in the Liberal party, thirty-two in the Progressive Conservative party, ten in the C.C F. group, three 'in the Social Credit group and two among the independents.
But the composition of the committee is to be thirty-three from the Liberal party, sixteen from the Progressive Conservative party, six C.C.F.'ers, three Social Crediters, and two from the eight independents in the house.
That division was proposed in a letter which I. as C.C.F. whip, received from the chief government whip, the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir). The letter, referring to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), states:
He has asked for a committee of sixty members. On the basis of the arrangement made by the steering committee this would provide for six members from the C.C.F. party membership.
I presume that similar letters went to the whips of the other parties. I quote that paragraph from the letter of the chief government whip only to indicate that the basis taken for the composition of this committee is that which the so-called steering or striking committee had arrived at with respect to another matter, namely that of standing committees.
I submit that has nothing to do with this matter. In fact, as a member of the striking committee I was told in that committee that any decision we made there with respect to the standing committees did not have any bearing upon the composition of other special committees to be set up by the house. However, it is quite clear from the letter I have just read, and also from the names in the motion now before us-and the party designations of the hon. members mentioned are easy to identify-that the basis chosen in this instance is the one arrived at by the striking committee-not, may I say, by unanimous decision-for the standing committees.
That basis, if I may place it before the house, is that the Liberals shall have fifty-five per cent of the membership of all committees, the Progressive Conservative party twenty-five per cent, the C.C.F. 10-8 per cent, the Social Credit group 5-1 per cent and the independents 3-1 per cent.
Against that list of percentages, which total 100 per cent, let me remind the house that the number of members in the various groups
in the house entitle those groups to the following percentages on all committees: Liberals, 52-7 per cent; Progressive Conservatives, 27-3 per cent; C.C.F. 11-4 per cent; Social Credit, 5-3 per cent; Independents, 3-3 per cent.
I shall not discuss the matter of standing committees at this time. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, you might rule me out of order if I were to continue that part of the discussion any further. We are being asked to set up a committee on the basis of a division which was communicated to the whips of the various parties-

times unworkable, that you can get better work done by a committee of twenty or fifteen members and sometimes a committee of two or even one is a good idea, if it is the right man. mittees set up by the house, and I think most people will agree with that. I was sorry to hear the parliamentary assistant to the minister become a little political in his remarks the other night. Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS' POULIOT (Tem-iscouata):	Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the minister upon the choice of an assistant, who has been a member of this house for a number of years and has shown a knowledge of what he is speaking about. for gratuities. Here is the second thing. Yesterday the Princess Louise Dragoon Guards were received in Ottawa with the beating of drums and a fine procession. This resolution provides that a select committee be appointed to consider all legislation passed since the commencement of the war, relating among other things to the treatment of returned men. When the treatment of returned men is being considered by this committee I hope that it will do all in its power to see that soldiers who have returned from the war suffering from nervous diseases are not placed in provincial insane asylums. I hope that it will see that suitable military hospitals are provided for these men and that they are not put into provincial hospitals which are occupied by the insane and which are sometimes very much overcrowded. I know it is said by some people that these men can get better treatment in provincial hospitals. I question if that is true of many of our provinces. I know that if I were the parent of a man who had returned from overseas suffering from a nervous condition I would not want to see him put into one of those institutions. Returned men should have their own hospitals.
There is another matter to which this committee might give some attention. I am not satisfied that veterans who are patients in our military hospitals invariably get the best of treatment and advice. I have in mind the case of an infantry soldier who was in hospital in Italy. He was brought back t-o this country suffering from some disease and was placed in one of our military hospitals. He has been there for months, and his condition has not improved, in fact, if anything it is getting worse. I wrote the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) about this matter. He assured me that he would look into it, and I appreciate that he is doing so. But I have seen this veteran on one or two occasions, and I have thought, when I have talked with him and considered his condition and tried to find out something about it, that if I were his father I would be far from satisfied with the treatment that boy was receiving, that I would want to have specialists called in to advise as to the best treatment. I may be mistaken, but I do not think in these military hospitals' we have such specialists, and I do not know if provision is made

There should be provision that they can be called in, and I would urge the committee to see to it that in military hospitals there be provided or made accessible specialists in cases where particular treatment is needed or in what I may term obstinate cases where the condition of a returned man is not any too well understood by the staff of the hospital.

May I direct another question to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yesterday President Truman told congress that he would initiate discussions with Canada and Great Britain looking towards international cooperation in the control of atomic energy, and called on the world to outlaw the atomic bomb. In the meantime he intimated that the secret of the new bomb would be preserved within the group of Great Britain, Canada and the United States. Have there been any discussions of a formal or informal nature between the governments of Canada and the United States of America with regard to the points covered by President Truman in his message to congress? If so, does the government of Canada hold views similar to those which he so expressed at that time?
A further question is this: Is Canada proposing to institute a body similar to the United States atomic energy commission, which appears to be clothed with wide and special powers to direct and control atomic energy experimentations? May I also ask, in view of the importance of the subject, when it is anticipated that the discussions, which President Truman mentioned, among this group of powers will be initiated, and who will represent Canada in those discussions?
Atomic Energy

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): With respect to the last portion of my hon. friend's question, no previous notice had been received and I am not in a position to make any statement at this moment. As to the earlier portions of his remarks and questions, the full context of President Truman's message to congress of yesterday has not yet been received in Ottawa, and I am not prepared to comment upon it until we have an opportunity to examine it closely. I can say now that there have been discussions with officers of the government of the United States over a considerable period dealing with the development and employment of atomic energy. The Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) has been a member of a combined policy committee, which was established in August, 1943, the other members of which were Mr. H. L. Stimson, then United States Secretary of War, Doctor Vannevar Bush and Doctor James B. Conant for the United States, and the late Field Marshal Sir John Dill and Colonel J. J. Llewellin for the United Kingdom. It was a committee of the highest level dealing with the research work and experimentation that were being carried on.
The present representatives of the United Kingdom on this committee are the Earl of Halifax and Field Marshal Sir Henry Wilson. Consideration is being given to the most effective organization to be adopted in Canada for the further study of Canadian policy and activities in this field, and I hope that in this connection a further announcement may be made before long.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is customary for ministers of defence when presenting their estimates to make a statement concerning the activities of the various forces.
In making a statement to-day concerning the Royal Canadian Air Force, I realize that this will be the last report to parliament on the wartime activities of the force.
Under the circumstances, for the benefit of the members and also for record purposes, I would like to give a short resume of the war record of the R.C.A.F., its present position and the plans for the future.
My remarks may well be divided under the headings yesterday, to-day and to-morrow.
On August 31, 1939, slightly over six years ago, the Royal Canadian Air Force had a total permanent strength of only 3,048 officers and men. In addition there were 1,013 all ranks in the auxiliary air force.
With the outbreak of war the air force forged ahead-taking on additional commitments and rapidly increasing the number of its airfields and personnel. Strength grew from the 3,048 of September to a peak of 232,585, of which 17,412 were civilians-not in uniform. From this peak the numbers decreased, until on V-E day the total was 181,489, of which 11,015 were civilians. In the intervening period the R.C.A.F. had suffered casualties totalling 21,866, of which 6,615 were fatal, 8,836 have been officially presumed dead, 1,526 are missing, 1,376 were seriously wounded or injured, and of the prisoners two are unaccounted for in Europe, three not yet officially reported upon in the far east, and the remainder were either reported missing and have since been found to be safe, or were prisoners of war either released, escaped or repatriated under the Geneva convention.
The first major step in the development of the air force was the signing of the British commonwealth air training agreement in Ottawa on December 17, 1939, by Great Britain, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. By this instrument the dominion became the operating partner of the most extensive training programme which, up to that time, had ever been developed. The Royal Canadian Air Force acted as general manager in this programme, and as a result of this heavy commitment the main role to be played by the force in the early days of the war was deter-

Demobilization-Air Services
mined. For many months that role was to be mainly training rather than operation, and so it was only a token operational force which was despatched overseas in the early days of the war. It was not until late in 1940 that the original three squadrons were reinforced by the first graduates from the training plan-the first trickle in the flood which was to mount to the tremendous total of 131,553 graduates before the termination of the plan, and of these 72,835 were members of the R.C.A.F. Of the total figure 49,808 were pilots; 29,963 navigators of various categories; 15,673 air bombers; 18,496 wireless operator-air gunners; 14,996 straight air gunners; 1,913 flight engineers, and 704 naval air gunners.
Following the termination of the B.C.A.T.P. agreements on March 31, 1945, a special agreement was entered into with the government of the United Kingdom to provide for the continuation of training for a limited number of R.A.F. personnel at R.C.A.F. schools in Canada. The costs of training these men were borne by the United Kingdom. After V-J day this, too, was concluded and the last graduating class was "winged" on September 7. During the short life of this supplementary plan 1,211 airmen graduated, of which 465 were pilots and 746 navigators and navigators B. All but fifty-seven were members of the Royal Air Force.
The three squadrons of the R.C.A.F. which had been sent to the United Kingdom in 1940 *were unable to absorb the ever-growing stream of R.C.A.F. personnel who graduated from the plan, and as a result the vast majority of the early Canadian graduates were posted to R.A.F. unite. Throughout the war there were always many more Canadians serving overseas with R.A.F. units than with R.C.A.F. units.
With the large numbers of R.C.A.F. personnel arriving in the United Kingdom the expansion of Canada's operational organization became highly desirable. Differences in pay entitlements, service conditions, trade divisions and other important factors in the life and careers of R.C.A.F. airmen, as compared with personnel of the R.A.F., complicated administration both for the R.C.A.F. and for the R.A.F. Accordingly additional R.C.A.F. units were formed to absorb a percentage of Canadian aircrew, and long before hostilities ceased, forty-eight R.C.A.F. squadrons were fully operational overseas. Under the original plan these were to be R.A.F. units in everything other than name and nationality of aircrew, ill groundcrew were to be found by the R.A.F.

until such time as sufficient personnel could be released from the B.C.A.T.P. schools and posted overseas. The ultimate aim was of course to have R.C.A.F. squadrons, manned fully by Canadians-both aircrew and ground-crew-by the process which came to be known as Canadianization. Though this goal was never fully reached, at the cessation of hostilities in Europe, the percentage of Canadian groundcrew in our overseas squadrons was uniformly high.
The magnificent record of these Canadian squadrons is now a matter of history, as is the "record of the other thousands of R.C.A.F. personnel who did all their operations with the R.A.F.
The most famous of Canada's air formations was of course the No. 6 Bomber group of Bomber command; and the famous Vancouver Pathfinder squadron of the same command. During the last year of the group's operations, under the command of Air Vice-Marshal C. M. McEwen, C.B., M.C., D.F.C., records were broken again and again and the Canadian squadrons established a reputation second to none in Bomber command. During the war the Canadian heavy bomber squadrons carried out 48,927 sorties in 262,982 operational flying hours, and dropped 125,575 tons of bombs on Europe.
They established a record surpassed by no other formation. They produced men in every way worthy to take their places in the hall of fame, alongside the heroes of the first world war.
In this last war, just as in the first world war, Canadians also excelled as fighter pilots. R.C.A.F. fighter squadrons flew 144,851 sorties in 212,148 operational flying hours, and destroyed 1,241 aircraft, probably destroyed 142 and damaged a further 607. The unit scoring the largest number of successes was the famous city of Edmonton squadron, the aircrew of which knocked down 169 Germans, and destroyed 82 flying bombs.
From October 1, 1944, to the termination of hostilities in Europe our fighters flew 26,163 sorties and lost 144 aircraft. But during that period they destroyed 236 enemy aircraft and made 1,600 cuts in vital nazi rail communications. They also destroyed 958 vehicles, 516 railway cars and 92 locomotives and damaged an additional 632 locomotives. In addition they either destroyed or damaged two mediumsized ships, one cruiser, six E-boats, 97 barges and 40 tanks.

Demobilization-Air Services
Our coastal command squadrons, also, established a magnificent record. Their role was not spectacular, but day after day-night after night-virtually twenty-four hours a day- our men, to use their own expression, "stooged" over the ocean-in all kinds of weather, keeping the sea lanes of the world open for united nations shipping. From this side of the Atlantic our squadrons based in eastern Canada and Newfoundland provided protection for shipping on the northwest Atlantic. Their patrols took them to mid-ocean and frequently required them to be diverted to Iceland, the Shetlands and even to the British isles. During these operations our aircrews flew 25,500 sorties [DOT]in 175,000 operational flying hours and made 69 attacks on U-boats. It was on this work that the late Flight Lieutenant David E. Hornell won undying fame-and the Victoria Cross.
The R.C.A.F. transport units, formed late in the war, also established records. One Canadian squadron, based in Burma, flew more operational hours, more sorties and carried more freight than any other similar unit in the R.A.F.-and that record still stands.
From the outbreak of war to the 15th of September last, members of the R.C.A.F. were awarded 7,107 decorations including one Victoria Cross, 66 Distinguished Service Orders, 3,481 Distinguished Flying Crosses and 484 Distinguished Flying Medals. I have here a complete list of dceorations and commendations awarded to members of the R.C.A.F. and Canadians in the R.A.F. for services in the war, which I will table at the conclusion of my remarks.
Canadians in the R.A.F. received a total of 356 awards including one Victoria Cross to the late Squadron Leader Bazalgatte, 16 D.S.O.'s, 196 D.F.C.'s and 24 D.F.M.'s.
I shall also table the names of all those personnel decorated subsequent to the list tabled on April 4, 1945.
Following the cessation of hostilities in Europe the R.C.A.F. was called upon to take part in the occupation of Germany. Our quota consists of a force of about 10,000 made up of two heavy bomber squadrons; four fighter squadrons with wing headquarters; three medium range transport squadrons, equipped with Dakota aircraft and, until December 31, 1945, one Liberator long range transport squadron. These transport squadrons are controlled by a wing headquarters based in England. At the present time the transport squadrons, two of which were previously based in India and Burma, are occupied in regular transport
duties, including repatriation of liberated prisoners of war and other personnel from the East. The Liberator and two of the Dakota squadrons, based in the United Kingdom are assisting in this work between Karachi and the United Kingdom. Also included in the occupational force are those personnel who are employed on the control commission and for the disarmament of Germany, on both of which tasks certain positions have been allotted to the R.C.A.F.
After the defeat of Germany our attention turned to the Pacific, and a force was mobilized for service in that area. To make up this force eight heavy bomber squadrons from No. 6 group flew across the Atlantic to the east coast of Canada and began training for the new theatre of operations. It had been intended to equip these units with Lincoln aircraft-an improvement on the Lancaster, which had served our squadrons so well in the latter days of the European war-but the early capitulation of Japan, put an end to these preparations, and six of these squadrons have now been disbanded.
The two units still being retained are continuing a programme of training designed to keep them in a state of efficiency. They will form part of the post-war organization of the R.C.A.F. and will provide the necessary defence for our shores in addition to the air sea rescue activities which are part and parcel of all coastal operations.
General demobilization is now proceeding with all possible speed and has of course been materially increased since V-J day. All surplus personnel of the R.C.A.F. are being released on a first in-first out basis, with overseas service counting double.
In addition, where the exigencies of the service permit, personnel may be released on application in the following cases:-
(a)	Prospective employers may make application for the release of key personnel to provide for the expeditious and effective reconversion of industry from war-time to peacetime production and the maintenance of maximum employment. In those cases where the industrial selection and release board recommends release, appropriate action is taken by the R.C.A.F. wherever possible.
(b)	Personnel in Canada who produce satisfactory evidence that they are entitled to be reinstated in their former employment, in accordance with the terms of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, and who intend to return to such former employment.

Demobilization-Air Services
(c)	Personnel in Canada who provide satisfactory evidence that they will undertake or resume farming operations where there is need of their services. This includes personnel now on farm leave without pay.
(d)	Personnel in Canada who intend to proceed with university or other similar educational studies, provided satisfactory evidence is produced that they have been accepted for training at a university or similar institution.
(e)	Personnel transferring to other armed forces.
(f)	Personnel whose release is authorized on compassionate grounds.
(g)	Personnel who have attained their forty-second birthday.
(h)	Personnel who apply for release to resume school teaching.
The following personnel are being released regardless of their priority points:
(a)	Married personnel of the women's division and the nursing service.
(b)	Over-age officers.
(c)	Personnel medically unfit for operational flying.
Personnel serving overseas are being repatriated in accordance with their point score which is based on both total length of service and length of service overseas. They are all being released on arrival in Canada with the exception of those in certain administrative ground trades where existing shortages necessitate their continued employment in Canada.
From V-E day to 1st October, 37,907 R.C.A.F. and W.D. personnel were repatriated to Canada from overseas. Of these 6,455 were repatriated from September 1 to October 1, inclusive.
Between V-E day and the official announcement of V-J day 17,556 service personnel had been retired or discharged and the number of civilians employed had been reduced by 1,108. From V-J day to September 30, 37,396 left the service, and during September alone 30,627 passed through the release centres into civilian life, or over 1,000 per day.
At the present time the strength of the R.C.A.F. stands at 124,052 made up of 27,910 overseas and 96,142 in Canada, of which 9,109 are civilians. Of those in Canada 28,071 are awaiting release.
It has been realized that rapid demobilization would be most dangerous unless certain steps were taken to prepare air force men

and women for their new role, and to make the transition from service to civilian life as painless as possible. It is hardly necessary to remind the house of the extensive system of personnel counselling, which has been in operation in the R.C.A.F. for many months. Every person being retired or discharged from the Royal Canadian Air Force is interviewed by a personnel counsellor and his or her aptitude for particular civilian occupations is gauged. This is no haphazard matter, but a scientific assessment of the qualities and technical skills of those interviewed so that they may be advised as to the type of employment to which they are best suited.
In addition to the personnel counsellors we have the education officers, who conduct courses in all units, and thus implement the advice of the counsellors. Interested personnel may improve their education or their technical skill and fit themselves for better and more interesting work on demobilization. With these two aids it is safe to predict that a very large percentage of demobilized personnel of the R.C.A.F. have improved their qualifications during their service careers.
Concurrent with the demobilization of personnel of the R.C.A.F. has gone the closing of schools, units and stations. During the peak of the commonwealth air training plan we had 100 schools and 182 other units established across Canada.	[DOT]
Following the termination of the B.C.A.T.P. agreement, schools utilized under the plan have been progressively closed. Of the major training schools, there were still twenty-nine open at V-E day.
Immediately following the cessation of hostilities in Europe steps were taken to reduce the number, and at V-J day the twenty-nine schools had been reduced to seventeen.
The collapse of Japan brought further drastic reductions so that at the moment only four major schools remain open, pending the establishment of an interim force.
Cuts in the operational units have been no less drastic. On V-E day there were twenty-six operational squadrons in Canada made up of twelve bomber reconnaissance, three fighter, three composite, three transport, two communications, two ferry and one operational training. On the 30th of September only nine remained made up of two long range bomber reconnaissance, three transport, one ferry, one communication and two photo squadrons. One of these transport squadrons will be disbanded next month.

Demobilization-Air Services
Operational stations have also been closed, so that now only five of the original twenty-four remain.
With the closing of stations and disbanding of units much equipment becomes surplus to immediate needs. The amount of equipment to be retained as a reserve is based on an estimate of five years requirements. The stock position at all equipment depots is checked by the procurement branch so that surpluses are ascertained and disposed of. Storage of this reserve equipment is provided at reserve equipment maintenance units established across the country.
In disposing of properties the stations are first placed at the disposal of the other services. If not required for the operations of these departments, the property concerned is declared surplus to requirements and, (a) in the case of leased property, returned to the owners, or (b) if purchased property, turned over to Crown Assets Allocation Committee for reference to other government departments including the Department of Transport, and if not required, turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal.
Surplus equipment is treated in a similar way.
I should like to make it quite clear that there is nothing sinister in our methods of disposing of surplus equipment or supplies. There appear to be some people who have the impression that anything we no longer require we destroy, and I should like if possible to disabuse their minds of this matter.
In a highly technical force like the air force it is inevitable that scientific skill will constantly produce new and improved equipment. As new developments appear old models become obsolete, and in war time we cannot afford to send our boys into the air with anything but the most modem equipment available.
As a result much equipment becomes surplus to requirements-sometimes because it is obsolete, sometimes because it is worn out or damaged, and sometimes both, but in every case careful consideration is given as to the disposal of this equipment, and disposal of it is made through War Assets Corporation.
While we are still engaged in the process of demobilization it is realized that with the end of the war plans must be prepared for our post-war forces.
No definite decision has yet been made as to the strength and composition of the postwar air force, as until the nature and extent
of any commitments that we may have under international or regional agreements have been determined it is obviously impossible to reach any final decision.
In the meantime plans are being prepared to provide Canada with a balanced force which would be capable of rapid expansion should the necessity arise.
The proposed post-war organization will be made up of three parts:
(a)	Regular
(b)	Auxiliary
(c)	Reserve
The regular force should comprise all branches of air force activities including bomber, fighter and transport squadrons, together with the necessary ancillary units, and for this purpose a strength of from 15,000 to 20,000 personnel is planned.
The auxiliary force will be made up of squadrons based at strategic points throughout the dominion and corresponds to the militia units of the army. These squadrons will provide opportunities for our young men to qualify for their wings or to secure training in their groundcrew trades.
The reserve will be made up of qualified air and ground personnel who in an emergency may be recalled for further service. Meanwhile, like the members of the auxiliary force, they will continue their normal peace-time occupations.
In planning for this post-war organization, arrangements are being made to perpetuate squadrons which took such an important part in the downfall of Germany. These will be localized as far as possible in the districts with which they were affiliated during their service overseas.
The production of the atomic bomb will no doubt have far reaching effects on the whole science of war, but whatever its effects may be upon the other services, I consider that it will undoubtedly increase the relative importance of air power.
The new field of atomic energy has introduced a situation which will require increased attention being paid to aeronautical research. This research will be imperative if the R.C.A.F. is to keep in line with changing conditions and -by the pooling of research findings-abreast with the developments in the specialized field of aviation.
With this in mind a division of research and development has been established within the force, which works in close cooperation with the other services and the National Research Council.
Demobilization-Air Services

One of the most important fields of research for which Canada is especially suited is in the sphere of cold weather operations. Much experimental work was carried on in this direction during the war period, and it will be continued in the days of peace. Information gained in this way is not only valuable to the service but is of benefit to civil aviation generally.
It would perhaps be of interest to hon. members to learn of the work at present being carried on by one of the R.C.A.F. units known as the radio wave propagation unit.
Canada's proximity to the north pole and its consequent position in the auroral region carries with it not only the advantage of being the centre of global airways, but also the disadvantage of giving the dominion a condition involving certain radio black-out spots. This condition is peculiar to Canada. The danger of these black-out spots to navigation can readily be appreciated. In an endeavour to combat this condition a radio wave propagation unit to forecast workable radio frequencies is now in operation. The research is being carried out, and will be continued, to determine the effect of the auroral zone, and to adjust predictions accordingly. Ionospheric recording units, by means similar to radar, record hourly the conditions affecting radio transmissions in the ionospheric layers, that is the space stretching from 40 to 260 miles above the earth's surface. This data is correlated with that of actual operating conditions and analysed. By these means predictions of workable frequencies may be made so that contact may be maintained on all wireless circuits at all times.
As a result it will be possible to ensure the most efficient use of equipment and radio facilities. The importance of this service in the saving of personnel, ships and aircraft cannot be overemphasized.
There is one particular division of the R.C.A.F. of which I want to make special mention, and that is the Women's Division.
While no decision has as yet been reached as to the employment of women in the permanent air force, I should like to express the' appreciation of the Department of the outstanding part played by the Women's Division throughout the war.
The Women's Division is the pioneer women's service organization in Canada, and has proved itself equal to every test to which it has been put. Those tests were neither few

nor simple. Arduous-and in many cases heavy-work has been undertaken cheerfully, and carried out carefully and efficiently.
Though precluded from flying duties, these women, recruited "so that men might fly" have been of inestimable service to the R.C.A.F. and to Canada. The Department of National Defence for Air joins all of Canada in saying "Thank you" for a job magnificently done.
Pending the determination of the composition of the permanent air force an interim force has been authorized, covering the period to September, 1947. For this force, which will operate under active service status, volunteers are being accepted both from serving personnel and from those who have been transferred to the reserve.
This interim force in addition to providing personnel for our occupation squadrons and home establishment, will also be used as a proving ground for personnel. These two years will give our officers an opportunity to evaluate the fitness of personnel for the peacetime role of the R.C.A.F. and at the same time enable those who join to decide if they wish to make a career in the service.
While persons who do not elect to serve in this interim force will not be barred from appointment to the permanent force, those who do enroll will be in a favourable position for permanent appointment.
In presenting the cash requirements for the R.C.A.F. for the current year, it will be seen that the cessation of hostilities has enabled me to revise my previous estimates and to make material reductions below the requirements for the previous year.
As compared with the sum of over $1,090000,000 voted for the last fiscal year, the requirement this year is slightly over $598,-
400,000,	or a decrease of 45-4 per cent.
The major saving is made in the commitment for the maintenance of overseas squadrons, where there is a reduction of over $216,000,000.
A comparative statement of cash requirements for the last fiscal year and for this year has been prepared and is available for members of the house.
While, with the coming of peace, reduction in the strength of the R.C.A.F. becomes inevitable, the same spirit of initiative and enterprise within the service will continue to maintain the high standard of performance which is characteristic of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
