speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I think I had better say something on the point raised by the hon. member who has just taken his seat.

I should like, to make a few comments before the minister speaks. I believe that the two hon. members who have spoken at great length have been working on the wrong premise from start to finish. At page 551 of Hansard of September 28 are to be found the estimates and the amount already granted. That does not necessarily mean the amount already spent. Consequently I believe, as I have already stated, that the premise-upon which these hon. members have been spoken is incorrect. If I remember correctly, the government asked for two appropriations totaling somewhere in the neighbourhood of S2 billion, and the amount that was actually allotted or granted to the air service was S325 million. That amount has been broken down, but this first column does not mean that the amount was actually spent. Would the minister be good enough to break down for us at this time the amount that was actually spent during the first five months of the year out of the amount, that we granted as an allocation up to the present time?

I think the hon. member who has just sat down is referring to a table at page 551 of Hansard where there are three columns of figures. The first column is "amount already granted". The way I interpret that is that it covers the expenditures for five months and that the second column gives the extra amount which the minister expects will be required for the remaining seven months. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
When the original estimate was put in for this year we were allotted funds for five months, based on the estimates of the previous year. The fact that the average monthly expenditures for the last seven months of the year would appear to be greater than those in the first five months is no indication that our expenditures are increasing, as the hon. member for York South has suggested. When the accounts are actually paid, whether it be early or late in the year, is no indication that a considerable saving is not being made in the department throughout the whole fiscal year.
I have placed on the table, although I do not know whether copies have been distributed or not, a comparative statement showing the cash requirements for the year 1944-45, and also the cash requirements for the year 194546 for the various items. This table indicates the over-all saving which is being made in the

whole fiscal year, and shows a reduction of some forty-six per cent in the requirements for this year. Of course in the early part of the year we had commitments for large expenditures; the war was by no means over. We had commitments which had to be paid. In many cases they were not paid for in the first five months of the year; consequently they are outstanding and will have to be paid in the second part. I think in dealing with these estimates by far the most satisfactory method is the one we have adopted in the past of dealing with them item by item, and getting an explanation on each item as we reach it, rather than for each hon. member to go through the whole list and deal with his criticism of the various items, without making any progress. If that meets with the approval of the committee I suggest that the Chairman call the items, one by one, and we can deal with them in rotation.

With all deference to the minister, may I say that the other day the Minister of Finance gave us this statement of figures. I think the house ought to understand what they are supposed to mean. If the minister will look at page 551 of Hansard he will see what is perplexing the hon. members over here who raised the question, and what is in my mind. Does the first column not mean what the minister thought his requirements would be for the first five months of this year when the amount asked for was $2,000 million? Hon. members are entitled to think that is still what is meant. When the second column is put in, showing the ddi-tional amount required to March 31, 1946, we are entitled to think that is what is required for the last seven months. That is what is the matter with the situation, and that is what these hon. gentleman have been discussing. Maybe the minister could make it clear; what do these columns mean? And if they do not mean anything, why were they given to us?
What were they five-twelfths of?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The first amount voted in the last session of the last parliament was five-twelfths of the requirements for the year, based on the estimates of the previous year. We had not got our estimates for this year ready at the time that that amount was voted.

Could the minister tell us, for example, how much money has been actually spent during the first five months of this year on civil salaries and wages? Is the minister in a position to give us that informa-

Demobilization-Air Services
tion to-night, so that we can compare his figure with the figure which is shown at page 551 of Hansard, namely, $6,294,610?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has suggested that the committee might consider the statement item by item. In previous years, before going into the items, a certain latitude has been allowed for general discussion. I am wondering if the general discussion has been completed.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then, would it be agreeable to hon. members to have the committee continue with the general discussion? This would not preclude the asking of questions of the minister. When the general discussion is over we could consider the items individually.
In order to guide the discussion along the proper lines I think it is necessary for us to clear up the point as to what the three columns on page 551 of Hansard actually mean.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I should like to give the committee that information. The amount required for the whole year for civil salaries and wages is $12,094,320. The amount voted for the first five months of the year was $6,522,000, and what was actually expended amounted to $6,294,610.
Then the figures at page 575 are not correct. The second set of figures the minister gave did not correspond with the figures found at page 575.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The
$6,522,000 was the money voted. The amount shown as being already granted is the amount that has been released by the treasury board from the amount voted.

That cannot be correct, because if hon. members will look at page 551 they will find that the total amount we voted for the air force was $325,985,039. We find those same figures at page 549. Under the heading "air services" we find those exact figures. Then, right at the bottom of page 573 is a figure of $2 billion, the amount of the apportionment for the first five months of the year.

If I might make a suggestion, I think the minister could clear this up. As I see it, the first column is the allocation of the portion of the $2 billion that was allowed the airforce for these special items. The minister has indicated that he has the actual expenditures for those five months under each of those headings. I suggest that the committee ought to have the actual expenditures
under each of these headings for the whole estimates-not only for the estimates that are here, but the actual expenditures from one end to the other in connection with all these estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The actual expenditures are available for four months. The amount released by the treasury board is for five months. However, I can tell the committee the actual expenditures under each item for four months.
If the minister could do that it would help the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the time of the committee for only a very few moments, not to discuss figures, but to discuss a principle. I wish to refer to the request made the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver South, which was supported by the hon. member for Nanaimo, a request which I thought was a very reasonable one. It was simply this, that in discussing the items for any of the services we should, if possible, have before us a statement for all the services.
So far as I know that request has never been referred to. It struck me as reasonable, and I should have thought that the common courtesy which is usually practised in this chamber would result in some reference to it. If it is impossible to have that done we should have been told why it was impossible. The reason for it seems to me to be this, that in a consideration of two or three departments which are so closely inter-related it would be desirable to know how they are inter-related, and it would enable us better to scrutinize expenditures. What did we, in fact, get to-night from the Minister of National Defence for Air? We got a statement which made us all very proud of what had happened during the last war. Secondly, we got a statement of the strength of the air force in the future. But we did not get any statement of the strategic position. We did not get any statement, so far as I know, of our relations with our allies, either within the empire or outside it, or with the United States.
We got no statement of the strategic position at all. There was only some reference to our position in North America, up near the north pole, and a reference to certain physical difficulties which that caused in connection with radar. But I submit to the committee that when we look forward to the situation which we face, which in spite of our hopes from the united nations agreement, we all
Demobilization-Air Services

realize, is a very dangerous situation, I submit that we who are here now should not be left to think in a vacuum.
We are told that the airforce will be 10,000 in strength. But I have no way of knowing whether it should be 10,000, or whether it should be the 30,000, which the hon. gentleman who did not make the speech last night is reported to have said.
I should like to submit with great deference -to the Minister of Reconstruction that we who are in this chamber are being very much put into the position into which a group of business men are put if someone came to them and offered them a proposition whereby they are asked to subscribe a large sum of money to a company. Then they are told that this company has close associations with another company, but are not told anything about what those associations may be. In the same way we are told nothing about the business of our enterprise; we are not told what its operations cover; we are not told what its objectives are to be, but we are just asked to put up a large amount of money, and to put it up blindly.
The estimate we are now discussing runs into something like S600 million, and in Muskoka-Ontario we think that is a lot of money. I am sure the Minister of Reconstruction would not put any such proposition before any group of business men to whom he might be trying to sell business; and I submit it should not be put up to us in that way.
I remember hearing the hon. member for Macleod saying the other day-and I greatly regretted hearing him saying it-that we ordinary members were just ciphers, and counted for nothing. I hope that it is not going to be true. We are being asked to act and to vote large sums of money without the slightest idea of what we are doing. As has been already suggested, I suggest with great deference and respect that these figures should be taken back. I do not say this because I want to argue about S5 or $10 here or there, but because I feel that when I come to vote hundreds of millions of dollars I should be given some intelligible basis for why it is being done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall we consider the
first item agreed to?

I waited until you rose, Mr. Chairman, hoping that the minister was going to reply to the many demands or requests that have been made in connection with this matter. I do not think the present situation is a new one. I believe it is connected with the situation raised during the last few days by the hon. member for Late

Centre and the hon. member for Kamloops. I think the present procedure is exactly in line with what they were complaining about. Like the hon. member for Macleod, I do not wish to be a cipher in this committee. I agree with what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said and I had the same thought before he voiced it. If this broad statement could not be given by one of the ministers of national defence, then I think it would be only a courtesy to this committee to tell us the reasons why a statement could not be made.
I do not believe the committee will be satisfied until the minister has considered that request. Everyone in the committee and everyone in the country knows it was a reasonable request. It is being commented upon from time to time by the press and I think it is time it was done. If the minister cannot make a statement he should explain why he could not give us a statement even in its more narrow aspects. This is a matter upon which the minister certainly can speak. I should like to refer briefly to some points upon which I have not been enlightened and upon which I think I should be enlightened if I am to vote sensibly upon these resolutions.
I have one short observation to make with regard to money. Along with other hon. members, I am concerned over the size of this vote, but I am concerned also about another fact. I want to know how much of this vote is for war purposes and how much will be used for a peace-time airforce. That is a very important matter. We are starting off with a great revolution in our airforce, and from the amount of money that is voted in the ensuing year we shall know what kind of airforce we shall have. The amount the government is providing this first year will give us a key to its intentions. We shall know from that what efficiency we may expect from our peace-time airforce.
Putting aside the question of money, I should like to refer to a few other things I expected to hear from the minister.	We
have been told that the airforce is going to be a force of 15,000 to 20,000 men. We got one little crumb out of his statement, that two of the eight Pacific heavy bomber squadrons are to be maintained. We are told that the remainder of the air force will be made up of bombers, fighters and transport planes. I do not suppose there is an hon. member who would not have knowm that even if the minister had not told it. Really all we know about this airforce, apart from the occupational force, is that we are going to have two heavy bomber squadrons. I hope

Demobilization-Air Services
we shall not leam of the specific size of our airforce from the newspapers to-morrow morning. We have not had it here to-night. So much for the specific size and the number of squadrons which give us some idea of what we may expect in the future.
There are many more matters to be considered. For instance, there is the question of policy. Is this force to be an operational force, plus a training force, or is it to be what it was before the war, a training force only? That is an important question and I am surprised that the minister did not tell us.
I go on again to mention a few other items. The minister mentioned the size of the regular force and told us there was to be an interim airforce for which people will be allowed to volunteer. This committee and the country want to know whether volunteers are coming forward for this interim airforce. We want to know the success he has had to date in getting recruits for this force, the name of which would drive away almost any recruit. It is a most unhappy name and I suggest to the minister that he change it.
Then we want to know if it is part of the policy to maintain a paratroop training field with the necessary aircraft suitable for that purpose. We have heard a great deal about the atomic bomb and we have heard about rocket and V weapons which are capable of shooting several thousands of miles. No one can say what the effect of that kind of thing will be. If I were charged with any responsibility in this matter I know that one of the things I would require would be paratroops who could be sent back to deal with the points from which these weapons are launched. That would be the best possible defence in the world against the atomic bomb or anything like that which might be in the hands of the enemy.
If we do not go on with paratroop training we shall be omitting one of the most vital things necessary in cooperation between the airforce and the army in any future war. I do not suggest that we have thousands of paratroops or that we have a large establishment, but I think the minister should give us some idea as to what arrangements are being made for th ecarrying on of this type of training. Perhaps he intends to discontinue it for a short time, and perhaps he can indicate to us that within ten months or a year it is the intention of the government to start again with this training.
The minister mentioned that the auxiliary airforce was to be set up again and I was pleased indeed that that is to be the case.
Many of us remember the auxiliary airforce that existed before this war. For_many years they used Tiger Moths, and it was only in the immediate months before the war that they had any operational type of aircraft. We should like to know from the minister how these auxiliary squadrons are to be equipped. Is preliminary training only to be given so that when war breaks out it will take months before they can become operational, or are aircraft to be supplied which are suited to their skills so that the force will be ready at once, as was the R.A.F. auxiliary during the Battle of Britain, to step right in and meet any threatened danger?
Before I sit down I would ask the minister to make a general statement upon this question, or if he would prefer it, although I do not want to do so, I would be prepared to ask him specific question after specific question until we obtain the information which I believe the committee is desirous of getting. I am not prepared to go on with any of these items until I hear from the minister as to the substance of this airforce and, as the hon. member for Muskoka^Ontario said, I am not prepared to go on in a complete and perfect vacuum. Here is a test of the charges that were laid at the door of the government the other day of legislating by order in council. Here is a request that they can easily grant, a request that commends itself to every member of the house. There are two ways of doing this business. One is to sit like an oyster and rely upon the majority to vote everything through. The other is the way which I am sure would commend itself more to all of us, namely, for the minister to stand before his peers in this house to whom he is directly responsible as the people's representatives and tell us what we wish to know, not because he must, but because he wants to take us into his confidence so that we may discharge our duties in an intelligent manner. I offer that alternative to the minister and I should be glad to hear from him upon the points I have raised.
Mr. Chairman-
I sat down expecting the minister to make a reply.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I would be very glad to reply now if lion, members would give me the opportunity.

Before the minister replies, may I say that I think we are at cross-purposes. I do not see these estimates in the way that my hon. friends see them. I may be wrong, but, if so, I should like to be shown. That we are considering these estimates when the year is half-way through

Demobilization-Air Services
instead of at the beginning of the year is on account of the peculiar circumstances this year. If We were discussing these estimates last March or last April, we would have before us the estimates for a whole war year, and the government would give us-at least we would ask for it-all the material that was available to enable us to compare the expenditures this year with those of last year. When these estimates were prepared, if I understand aright, they were prepared for. a war year. But now the war is ended, and part of the estimates cover that part of the year when we were at war and the remainder are required for the demobilization period and for the maintenance of whatever forces may be retained after demobilization takes place.
What my hon. friends are asking for now is something that could be asked for with a great deal of force when the house meets at the next session, but it does not seem to me possible that they can reasonably ask for or get the information they have been asking for to-night, because I doubt very much whether in the United States or in the United Kingdom or in any other country governments have their plans completely prepared for the armed forces that will be required between now and the next war, which we hope will never happen, or that this government is in a position to know just what forces will be necessary to keep our share of the peace in the new international order that is to be set up. I think that is the situation.
I can see no great difficulty in dealing with these estimates. The minister can tell the committee what the expenditures were in the four months or so for which he has an accounting of the five or six months for which we granted an appropriation. As to the remainder of the year he can, in my opinion, give the committee only a fairly approximate estimate of what will be required for the demobilization of the forces that are to be demobilized and for the forces that will have to be maintained. I do not think we should play with this thing. It is too important. If we do play with it, we shall be kept here and be unable to carry on the work for which this parliament was brought together.

Mr. Chairman, there are two things to consider. There is the question of audit, and the question of the use of the airforce. In two days the session will have lasted a month. The discussion that has taken place to-night has been the most informative since the beginning of the session, and I congratulate all the members who have spoken. I congratulate the hon. member for Nanaimo upon his change of tone He is older in years than I am but younger

in parliamentary experience, and I may tell him that a speech like the one he made to-night will carry him much farther than his first speech in this house.
During the war I looked at the estimates and I was not satisfied with them. I spoke of that to some business men, who could not understand them. I had the support of my very dear friend the hon. member for Davenport, one of the pillars of the Conservative party before he became a Progressive Conservative.
I surely have not slipped since, have I?

A pillar, a great man and a great explorer. Also my very dear friend the hon. member from Broadview, who has done more for the city of Toronto than any other living man. Those two hon. gentlemen supported my contention, and there were even editorials in the Ottawa Journal and in the Vancouver Sun to the effect that the views expressed by those hon. gentlemen were sound. What we suggested was that there should be a detailed account of the expenditures, and that simply because we were spending billions of dollars instead of hundreds of millions was no reason why we should not have vouchers. The point was, to build vaults if the ones which existed at the time were not large enough to contain all that stationery. The argument we made was that it was essential to the business of good government that everything should appear in the public accounts. Even though no one looked at them it was a protection, because those who handled the business would have known that anyone in this country, any man belonging to any party, could have found the details of expenditures in the public accounts. We carried on the fight; we were lone warriors- a Grit with two Conservatives-and we succeeded in getting something. I remember that one of the members for Lambton- Lambton-Kent, I think it was-asked the Minister of Finance if it was upon his suggestion that there had been a change in respect of the public accounts, and he said, "No; I am answering the member for Temiscouata." That is a long time ago. The hon. members for Davenport and Broadview and myself foresaw then what is happening to-day. During wartime very few members had the courage of their convictions about the public accounts. They forgot that the troubles we had in this country one hundred years ago about parliamentary government were on the question of dollars and cents; at that time it was pence and shillings. When it comes to public accounts there is not a citizen in Canada who has not the right to know how the money

Demobilization-Air Services
which comes from the taxes is spent. We fought that fight because we did not want parliamentary institutions to fall into disrepute; we wanted parliament to stand high in the minds of all Canadian citizens. That is the first point.
Of course the sound minds of so many gifted Canadians were blurred in time of war. Their conceptions of the true duties of a member of parliament were clouded, and they thought it was patriotism to vote money blindly. That is what happened. I do not blame the government for that; I blame the whole membership of the house, excepting a few, for having fallen so low through prejudice and passion as to forget the elementary duties of members of parliament. What the new members who were not parties to those debates and discussions are saying now is in fact an arraignment of the past. But they cannot blame the government for that. They may blame Arthur Meighen and R. B. Hanson and all the others who have been leaders of the Conservative party, just as they may blame the leaders of the Liberal party. But my hon. friends of the other groups cannot complain either, because they themselves fell in the trap. Was I not alone in denouncing from my place in the house a man who was connected with big business in Montreal, when he was running the Department of National Defence, and I said that he was a tool of international finance. My hon. friends of the Social Credit group, where were they? Discussing theories. They remind me of the fellow who drives his car and, seeing an obstacle in the way, instead of getting out to remove the obstacle and put it in the ditch, rises in his car and makes a speech to the obstacle: "O obstacle, disappear from my sight; let me proceed farther." They think their eloquence is so powerful that the log or stone will roll into the ditch. They are afraid to call a humbug by name.
The hon. member voted for the "obstacle", did he not?

Pardon me. Oh, I will describe to my hon. friend the obstacle I had. He came from Montreal; he was a Social Crediter; he was running in Temiscouata county, and he spent half of his time in canvassing in a neighbouring county thinking he was in Temiscouata. His address is Holy Grace street, Ville Marie, Montreal. He went back to Montreal, and we have not seen him in Temiscouata county. But he lost his deposit five or perhaps ten times over; I do not know.
Well, now, hon. members see what it is My hon. friend who has just spoken is just as
gifted as are all the sons of Erin, the emerald of the sea, the island of the saints. But the question is not who is gifted. I concede that my hon. friend is more gifted than I am. But when I was carrying on that fight I was alone;
I was alone with two Tories.
That too is reminiscent of the emerald isle.

We were fighting for responsible government, which dates back a long time before good Canadians were divided into Liberals and Conservatives. We were fighting for the principles for which my great-grandfather fought and voted, when he supported the ninety-two resolutions and afterwards helped Robert Baldwin after his fight in York to be elected in Rimouski. The principles for which my grandfather fought and my father fought are the principles for which I have been fighting. The question for me is not so much what happened in the past, but what is happening now and what will happen in the future. There is no use in crying over spilt milk. Everybody is responsible, and the important point is not to perpetuate the argument between those whom Swift-not Swift of the Canada Packers, but Swift the author- called the Big Endians and the Little Endians.
The minister now in charge of the department took it over after the conclusion of the war, and he inherited a very heavy legacy. I cannot understand why a greater tribute was not paid to Doctor Cyrus Macmillan, who was the back-bone of the department for air, for all the good which was done during the time that he was parliamentary assistant. A fine man, most unassuming and devoted to his task, he also honoured himself as chairman of most difficult committees like those on reconstruction and veterans affairs. He was making no noise but he was doing the work nevertheless. He was not alone, however, because there were others in the department, one of them in a swivel-chair, occupying the highest post, a group captain or a squadron leader. At any rate, he occupied the highest post although he was a man of no military training except for a Cook's tour of fifteen days in England. But he is the big bug of the department now, the nigger in the woodpile, an intriguer of the worst kind, a man of the old regime. I tell the committee, and the countiy will know to-morrow, that the big bug of the former regime is still the nigger in the woodpile in the air department, or one of them. There are eighteen million negroes in the Belgian Congo and I do not know how many there are in the woodpile of the department. But there they are and here we are, and they are flying everywhere, flying to files, flying to

Demobilization-Air Services
the doors, flying everywhere, but flying in Ottawa. And they are omnipotent. They decide about the length of the war.
It is my deep conviction that if the example of that great man who, although unknown in Canada, is well known in Europe, General Henri Guisan, the commanding officer of., Switzerland, has not been followed, there is a reason. What did General Henri Guisan do? In the month of August he decided to retire, because the war was over in Switzerland. But here it continued. It is impossible to get boys out of the airforce at the present time. There is one who was employed as a technician with the telephone company down home. He is sick; his health is bad. His family lives down there and he could be useful in the telephone company, but it is impossible to get him out of the airforce, where he does nothing, just on account of some commanding officer who wants to keep all his men around him to show how indispensable he is to the country. And we have to pay prebends to these parasites.
Brass hats.

I do not know whether he is a brass hat or not, but he is a parasite, and he is not alone. Here we see them in Ottawa, fellows with absolutely nothing to do, and girls who do nothing but who remain in the air force, because the number must be large enough to justify a continuance of the prebends to some big man, some big powerful man who has waged wars in Ottawa. They waged the war in Ottawa. Just before this war there were veterans of the South African war who were in office in Ottawa and who had waged also the first great war, and now they have been waging the second great war in Ottawa, not moving out of Ottawa. They do not travel on railways or in aeroplanes; they stick to their swivel-chairs. And they are heroes.
Well, sir, it is a serious matter, but there is a ridiculous side to it. Of course it is ridiculous to think of it. We are discussing two things at the same time. We are discussing the burden of taxation, but nobody uses the scissors in the right place to simplify our discussion. You know very well, Mr. Chairman, that so long as we have that large number of parasites in Ottawa and throughout the world-yes, I will say the world, because they are in Europe as well as in Canada-it will be impossible to reduce taxation. What struck me in the argument made by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was this. Speaking as a business man, he said he did not understand the whole thing. I agree with him. I cannot understand it either.
[Mr. Pouliot.J
We are, all of us, complaining of the burden of taxation, and we have reached the point where the people will not be willing to suffer taxation as we did during the war, now that the war is supposed to be over. There is not the same incentive to continue paying taxes, although we shall have the same amount of taxes to pay on account of the expenditures, and that has no raison d'etre at all. The continuation of war expenditures for the sake of those who did not go to the war is incredible.
There are two classes of those who did not go to the war and there is one class that deserves less sympathy than all others. That is the class of those who did not go to any theatre of war but who thought it was their duty to send others there; and those fellows are heroes, mark you, because they remained here in Ottawa or Toronto or Montreal or Quebec city or Winnipeg or Vancouver. They were everywhere.
And they got decorations.

Surely, by sitting still in their swivel-chairs, and perhaps by turning a little. When they turned to the right they got a decoration and when they turned to the left they got another decoration, because they could not move, so that when they made the least move they deserved a decoration. At this stage of the discussion I challenge all my colleagues to defend the brass hats, but I do not think one will rise in their defence.
Now, sir, can it go on any longer like that? Is it possible for the Canadian people to continue paying taxes, the same amount of taxation, now that the war with Italy, Germany and Japan is over, just as when the war was going on? I cannot believe it. A very important thing was said to my hon. friend the member for Davenport, the hon. member for Broadview and myself, during the war when we were asking for more information, and that was, "Oh, it is a war secret." It was a war secret! Well, are there any more war secrets now in connection with these expenditures, now that the war is over? And these expenditures are the same, exactly the same as when the war was still on. No change was made in them because the brass hats made their calculations to stay as long as possible in office and to continue to be the hidden power behind the throne. That is all. It is no secret; everyone knows it. But does anyone dare to say it? It is the truth acknowledged by everybody, but nobody says anything about it because they may have a friend there or a cousin or an uncle or a brother-in-law; they may have a son; I do

Demobilization-Air Services
not know what, but they may have somebody close to them and they are afraid to condemn that silly practice, just to protect a few friends, or because they are afraid to speak. That is the point. The other day I was unfair to the hon. member for Royal; 1 was too quick. Sometimes it happens to me. I regret it very much, because I give him credit for being a faithful member of the house. Besides that I cannot forget that he helped me, along with the hon. member for Vancouver South, on the civil service committee. I do not wish to offend any hon. member. Sometimes when I use strong language it is because of the depth of my conviction.
But the time is coming in the very near future when there will be a readjustment of feeling and of mentality, not only throughout the country but perhaps in this house too. It will be the great divide. When I was sitting on the other side of the house I spoke of a union opposition composed of all the-elements who were opposed to some fellows who were intriguers of the worst kind and who have since been discarded. I give credit to the Prime Minister for having discarded them. But now, sir, conditions are very serious in this country. The people think a lot, and deeply so. They are worried; they are worried about the future; and they make a distinction between those who are Liberals at heart, whatever their label may be, and those who have not the same understanding of things. I will not say any more about it tonight, but if it is necessary, and in the very near future, something may happen to be the occasion of that adjustment. All party labels may be discarded, may be thrown into the wastepaper basket, and there may be a readjustment not on party lines but on beliefs, on beliefs in the future of this country.
What is the privilege of a member of parliament? It is to be free; it is to be free of all ocular powers in Canada as well as anywhere else. The freedom of parliament is the most essential thing in this country. I consider it so important that I am ready to pass over many things that may displease me so as to find some ways and means to cut down that nefarious bureaucracy to a nonentity. Will it be done? I do not know, but it is a hard task. No one who considers the future of this country may see it in pink. The future is not rose; it is not pink. It will be very hard. We shall have to have the spirit of pioneers to meet our task.
Each member of parliament who was elected on June 11 knew very well that the future would be hard, difficult and most strenuous,
and that the hills to climb toward prosperity in this country were very abrupt. It was done just the same. It showed that each member and each candidate-I pay the same tribute to the candidates who were running, except to the imports that came to Temiscouata from Montreal and Quebec city-most of those who were running, and each one of those who was elected faced the future. At the time of their nomination and at the time of their election they knew very well that we were pretty far away from some of the easy times we had known before the war and before the depression, the easy times that followed the first great war and until 1929; far from it. The future is hard, and it will require more courage on the part of hon. members to take the necessary steps to face the future for the benefit of this country than was required when they accepted the nomination sometime before June 11.
It will take intelligence too.

My hon. friend has it. I
give credit to the hon. member for Lethbridge. He is liked by all hon. members. It is not so much a question of intelligence as of character, of determination, and of patriotism. That will be understood only by those who will not be ashamed or afraid to call Canada their country, and to call it their own country in the first place, and who will be good enough citizens to be proud to be good Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I may not be able to maintain the high level of debate that has been set by the previous speaker. There are some answers that I should like to give to points raised by various hon. members. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard asked me if I would give some indication as to what forces we were planning in the postwar period. I did not mention it before. It was not that I was trying not to put all my eggs in one basket when I made the report, but I do hesitate to make any definite pronouncement as to what our post-war forces will be, because obviously we cannot determine at the present time what we shall be required to provide. We do not know what international commitments we may have, and what those commitments may require from this country. But at the same time we are working on plans that are subject to change from time to time. In connection with the airforce we are planning at the present time on the basis of ten squadrons, of which four would be bomber reconnaissance, two fighter, three transport, and one photo. In addition
Demobilization-Air Services

to that, we would have communications flights and possibly some other small number of flights of other types of planes.
It may be said that that is not a balanced force. On the other hand we have the auxiliary squadrons that are being planned. That, too, is subject to change because it has been considered that any auxiliary squadron that is to function adequately must have a proportion of permanent force personnel attached to it in order to maintain and care for the aircraft which are on charge with that squadron.
I would hope to have at least in the neighbourhood of twenty auxiliary squadrons. They would probably be fighter squadrons, or equipped with fighter aircraft to a large extent, and, of course, trainer aircraft as well, which would mean that we would not need as many' fighter squadrons in our regular airforce in view of the fact that we would have fighter squadrons available from our auxiliary forces.
Then, of course, we have the reserve. I am not making any pronouncement as to what they will be called upon to do, or what we shall be able to do for them. I should like to see the reserve called up and given the opportunity for training each year. However, that is a matter to be decided in the future. I do not wish to be committed to any definite policy either as to auxiliaries or reserves until a considerably later day.
The hour is getting late, and I should like to mention again the question of figures, because it does not seem to me that some hon. members are clear as to what we have shown in the figures we have produced. As I said before, at the last session we got a supply vote of five-twelfths of the amount that had been voted in the previous year. All that money was not expended. While the five months supply that was voted amounted to 8453,876,000, the amount that was released by treasury board was 8325,985,039. All that amount was not actually paid out in cash, because a large amount of it is still on hand. But it was released by treasury board, and available to be paid out by the airforce.

Are the words "amount
already granted" as they appear in the first column of page 573 incorrect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: No. That has been granted by treasury board to the airforce; but that does not say that we have actually paid out that much money.
How much is on hand?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
For the
four months the actual expenditure amounted to $196,965,237. But the point I wish to make clear is this, that there is no use in going on a month-to-month basis, and averaging out our expenditures according to the amount we have spent in five months of the year. I would suggest that hon. members, from the schedules I have placed on the table of the house, make a comparison of the expenditures or requirements for the year 1944-45 with the amount asked for this year.
In 1944-45 the actual amount was $1,090 million. This year we are asking for 8598 million, which is, roughly speaking, about fifty-four per cent of what was voted in the previous year. Consequently, that is the comparison which should be made, and not the comparison as to what we were authorized to spend in five months, or what we actually spent in five months; because it is the overall commitment for the year that gives the indication as to whether we are actually saving money or whether we are being extravagant.

What purpose is served
by the first column on page 551 of Hansard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
It just
shows the amount released by treasury board to the department.
It is no good to us.
It just tangles us up.

I think every hon. member wishes to help the minister to get ahead with his estimates, to a point where he can give us whatever information he has concerning his expenditures. A short time ago some hon. member asked if the minister had the expenditures for five months in connection with the first item, and the minister answered. Then he said at a later time that he had the expenditures only for four months. I suggest that if the minister has the actual expenditures for four months he should give them to us to-morrow. Perhaps that is all he has and all he can give us.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
Possibly
I can obtain them for five months. I have them with me for four months, and I shall try to-morrow to have them for five.
If the minister could give us that, perhaps that is all he could give us.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The
increased fuel cost comes about solely because of methods which have been adopted for payment. During the time of the training agreements in Canada the fuel was being secured through lend-lease by Great Britain, and supplied by Great Britain as part of her contribution, so that we did not have to pay for it. Later on, there was a change in the method of providing fuel, and the cost of that item was consequently increased.
However, the actual consumption of gasoline in 1944-45 was 170,907,400 gallons. The estimated amount for 1945-46 is 66,278,800, showing a very great saving in the consumption of gasoline. The increase in that item is owing to the method adopted for payment.
That is why I should like to have the committee go through these items, one by one, so that explanations can be given in logical order. We would not have to go from one item to another and hop about without having full explanations of the various questions brought up. I should like to deal with each question fully when we come to each item.

As I said before, items Nos 9 and 10 go together. That is why we should have extra information in a properly prepared statement. If the minister could prepare another statement for to-morrow it would help a great deal.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned,
without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, October, 5, 1945.
